label: Learning at work
title: What will people learn at work?
paragraphs: Imagine joining a team where AI produces most of the analysis. Your job is to check it. How do you learn to spot a weak assumption if you rarely build an analysis yourself?

A job is also a place to develop judgment. I’m interested in how people acquire that judgment when more of their work arrives already done. Experienced staff face a related question: they may be able to correct an answer, yet have little say in which problem the system is solving.
Doing something yourself can look inefficient when a tool already has an answer. But that experience may be what prepares you for the next unfamiliar problem.
question: Which parts of a job should people keep practicing, even when AI can do them faster?

label: Thinking with AI
title: How can AI leave room for doubt?
paragraphs: I use AI in my own research. Imagine returning to a project after a few weeks away. A draft offers a neat explanation of the problem. You can follow the sentences, but you’re less sure why this explanation seemed right or what would make you give it up.

I’m interested in tools and working habits that help researchers stay with those questions. A useful system might help us revisit an uncertain choice or find an observation that doesn’t fit. It would also need to leave room for ideas that are still half formed.
Keeping track of every step can take attention away from the research itself.
question: What is the smallest amount of structure that helps people think together and take responsibility for a claim?

label: Cooperation between firms
title: What makes cooperation between agents worthwhile?
paragraphs: Consider two companies that could improve a shared service by connecting their AI systems. One has useful records, but sharing them could expose commercial knowledge. Even with a working connection, the company may see little reason to participate if most of the benefit goes elsewhere.

I’m interested in arrangements that make contributing worthwhile and give firms a say in how their knowledge is used. This becomes more demanding when agents can request information or act on it without a person negotiating every exchange. Technical choices about access and control then become part of the economic relationship.
question: What would make a company willing to keep contributing as the service and its participants change?

label: Organizing work with agents
title: What happens after the pilot works?
paragraphs: Imagine a team that uses an AI agent to draft replies to routine requests. People check every response. Later, the agent begins resolving cases and passing exceptions to colleagues. Who owns the outcome, and when should a manager change the agent’s remit?

I’m interested in this move from an isolated experiment to everyday work. Responsibilities may need to change across departments as people and agents adapt to each other. Giving someone responsibility for an agent’s work also raises a practical question: what authority and information do they need to exercise it?
question: Which decisions need explicit rules, and which depend on people developing new ways of coordinating as they gain experience with agents?
